title: The Stoat in the Orrery
markdown:
The wind, ancient and uninvited, tugged the tassels of Wizard Aster’s robe at the precipice of the Whispering Peaks. Below, the ravine held lanterns like lost fireflies along goat paths that clung to cliff. Higher, a city of rope bridges and timber stalls etched itself against stone.

Aster smoothed a crease in his tunic. “Remarkable. Truly. One imagines a creature of burrow and earth would favour cavities, hollow logs, even the forgotten husk of a wizard’s boot. Yet here we are.”

Pounce, a sleek russet stoat, was occupying a space he absolutely should not. Not a warm burrow. Not the dusty confines of an ancient spellbook. Not even the cozy husk of a discarded boot, which Aster had, in weaker moments, considered lining with felt. He had chosen his midday siesta deep in the carved workings of the Grand Orrery, a celestial model so exquisite that Aster, artificer of some renown, felt genuine dread at disturbing its cosmic harmony. One misplaced claw and Tuesday might arrive on a Thursday. A whisker showed between a brass meridian and a moon no larger than a thimble. It twitched in time with a gear that had never asked for company.

Wizard and stoat, paired, had reached an impasse that looked like clockwork.

“A calculated spell wants a predictable room,” Aster told the air. “A napping stoat consults other weather.” He adjusted moon-silver spectacles. “Specialized assistance, then.”

He descended toward the lower market, slow and deliberate, because hurrying on a goat path was how wizards became rumours. Wind whispered through bridge-rigging. A child sold roasted nuts in twists of bark paper. Someone argued the price of thyme as if thyme had committed a crime. If Pounce would be inaccessible, Aster would acquire tools, and perhaps something like a highly specialised badger, though he had reservations about neatness. He paused on a landing where the whole ravine showed itself, lanterns already rehearsing evening, and admitted, only to the wind, that he missed the weight of a stoat on his sleeve.

The market was a tapestry pinned to the cliff. Pomegranate and apricot banners snapped from tethers that seemed to dare gravity. Smiths clanged as if metal enjoyed the argument. Hardy mountain birds offered unsolicited opinions from the guy-ropes. A rope ferry creaked across a lesser gap, loaded with onions and one very dignified goat. Aster’s gaze, trained for faint magical signatures, found Griselda the Goblin Herbalist among roots like forgotten spells, fungi with inner light, leaves that held dew like tiny prisms. A jar of something that should not have been pickled sat in the shade and pretended innocence. Her obsidian eyes priced the world by whim, and by the moon, and by whether she liked your sleeves.

“Ah, Wizard Aster!” She cackled, pebbles down a slope. “Whispering Moss? Star-Glimmer for sleepless nights?”

“Good day, Griselda. I need a tool for delicate extraction. A miniature articulated claw. Precise grip.”

She rummaged and produced phosphorescent mushrooms, then a pair of glistening implements. “Moonpetal Dew-Graspers. Excellent for coaxing shy things. Seven shimmering river stones, and a promise to tell me the secrets of cloud-herding.”

Aster’s eyebrows rose a fraction. “Cloud-herding is weather, not a trade. And seven stones for tiny claws?”

“They are dew-kissed! The moon is plump. That adds two stones. Extra coaxing power.”

Aster paid, counting river stones that still remembered being river. Arguing with Griselda’s lunar moods was a longer errand than a stoat. He had tried, once, to explain meteorology. She had added a stone for the lecture. “And enticement? Something a discerning stoat cannot ignore? He has opinions about dried fruit, and stronger opinions about being lifted by the scruff.”

She winked. “A dried dream-berry. Rouses the stubborn. Three of my finest acorns, and a riddle answered.”

He handed over stones and acorns and began to shape a riddle about moons that napped in gears. A gruff boom interrupted from the next stall before the riddle could earn its keep.

“Rare finds! Magical amplification! Direct from the Underdark!”

A portly goblin in ostentatious silver rings held aloft a miniature mechanical arm, joints gleaming, pincer almost impossibly delicate. It looked exactly like the tool Aster had pictured in the moment before he had decided he did not want to picture tools that pinched stoats.

“The very thing!” the trader declared. Groknar, Aster recalled, a name that arrived whenever a wizard was about to spend less. His rings clinked a sales hymn. A velvet cloth was flourished and did not improve the price. “Groknar’s Grabber! Extracts treasures from nooks! A bargain at twenty gold! Nineteen if you look indecisive!”

A goat nearby looked indecisive on principle. Aster did not.

Aster looked from the arm to the Dew-Graspers. Impressive, yes. Convenient, suspiciously so. Groknar’s motive was coin. Griselda’s was the moon and whatever sparkled behind the pickled eyeballs.

“You cannot improve a plan,” Aster murmured, “without first making it stranger.”

Groknar missed the murmur. Aster understood the Graspers were for coaxing, not brute extraction.

“This arm is excellent,” he said. “My needs are more organic. Griselda, your Graspers coax. What if the subject is unmoved by dew?”

Griselda’s eyes narrowed. “Then one enhances the coaxing. Something that transcends the ordinary.”

“The dream-berry is promising. What if Pounce has an aversion to dried fruit? What if he prefers the scent of freshly unearthed moon-gems?”

“Moon-gems are rare. A shard can lure a shadow from its lair.”

“You have a way with rare things. This trader has a tool that may be overkill. A trade: your dream-berry, enhanced with a whisper of moon-gem essence, for a demonstration of the Graspers on a challenging subject.”

Groknar, scenting profit, revived. “Guaranteed extraction! It will not fail!”

Aster’s dismissive hand was unhurried. “Elegant for a brute problem. Griselda, a lure the most obstinate stoat cannot ignore, and I will pay in mushroom spores that glow blue on Tuesdays, and I will trade you that silver ferret figurine you have been coveting from afar.”

Her gaze flicked, almost not at all, to the figurine behind the jar of pickled eyeballs. The smile arrived slowly. “A symphony of scent. A siren’s call to the deepest slumberer.”

Wizard and stoat, paired, had always preferred a bargain to a grab.

Under the market’s watch, the pact was made. A small crowd collected, as crowds will when a wizard leans toward a jar of eyeballs. Griselda ground dream-berry with pulverized moon-gem on a slab that had seen stranger recipes, humming a reedy tune into the mountain air. The scent rose: sweet, mineral, a little like rain on a locked door. Groknar’s eyes sparked with the hope that Aster might yet prove a fool and come back for the Grabber at nineteen gold. A child asked if the stoat would be rescued by a dragon. Aster said the stoat would be rescued by patience, which disappointed the child and pleased the goat.

Aster did not look at Groknar. He looked toward the Orrery on its high terrace, a gold geometry holding one russet secret. Wizard and stoat, paired, had survived worse markets than this. He tucked the figurine’s promise into the trade and the pouch into his sleeve.

He climbed back with the pouch, past the same landing, past the same dignified goat, now returning without onions. The Orrery waited on its terrace like a patient constellation someone had taught to tell the time. Pounce was a russet comma among gold sentences. Aster did not shout. He did not prod. He did not conjure alarms. Groknar’s unused marvel stayed below, gleaming at nobody.

Then came the silent work.

Aster opened the pouch and let the scent drift into the gears. He waited. Wind found the tassels and left them. Lanterns below ticked from firefly to firefly. A raven crossed. The Orrery’s smallest moon completed a fraction of a degree, then another. A goat bell far down the cliff marked a sale. Aster did not speak. He did not name the fear of a bent axle or a stoat who preferred cosmos to kitchen. He held still the way one holds a cup too full. Starlight found a tooth of the largest gear and made it briefly kind. The lure smelled of forgotten caverns and the particular sweetness of a nap about to end. Dew-Graspers stayed in his sleeve, unneeded, a courtesy to the moon.

A twitch of russet. A whiskered head emerged, blinking, unconcerned. Pounce stretched, a sleek ripple, sniffed, and scampered down the gleaming framework to the pouch.

Aster knelt as if approaching a small emperor. Pounce chuffed, rubbed a leg, took the berry, nibbled with the concentration of a jeweller, and settled to groom his whiskers with profound satisfaction. A fleck of moon-gem dust rode one whisker and then did not. Aster stroked the sleek head and felt the Orrery, behind them, resume the private business of being a sky in miniature.

Wizard and stoat, paired, left the Orrery turning as it had been designed to turn.

Groknar’s Grabber stayed on the stall, a marvel with no audience. Aster bought a small useless trinket from him anyway—a tin star that pointed, with great confidence, at whichever pocket held it—a kindness that cost less than resentment. Groknar brightened enough to insult a neighbour’s onions. Griselda’s ferret figurine came out from behind the eyeballs and took the place of honour beside the Star-Glimmer. She did not charge Aster an eighth stone for watching.

Pounce rode home in the crook of Aster’s arm, dreaming, perhaps, of moons that did not mind being used as pillows. On the precipice Aster set him down long enough to check the Orrery’s smallest moon: still true, still turning, unchewed. The ancient wind found nothing left to tug but a tassel that had already decided to stay. Below, lanterns became evening in earnest. Aster climbed the last stair to his workroom, stoat aboard, and shut the door on extraction devices and lunar mark-ups alike.
characters: Aster (precipice wizard of the Whispering Peaks), Pounce (russet orrery-napping stoat), Griselda (goblin herbalist who prices things by whim)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
